query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is intended to retain the favorable mechanical performance of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi Cantor alloy while reducing cost and preserving a useful strength–ductility balance. Existing FeNiCrMn research has focused mainly on corrosion rather than dynamic loading. Molecular-dynamics studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys have examined temperature, strain rate, cracking, voids, and compositional variation, demonstrating condition-dependent mechanical responses, but they do not establish how to improve FeNiCrMn under dynamic loading. Given the constraints of remaining Co-free, controlling cost, and retaining balanced strength and ductility, what single intervention could improve the dynamic mechanical performance of FeNiCrMn over a defined range of temperatures and strain rates? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, the causal mechanism, a predicted outcome relative to unmodified FeNiCrMn, its boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing controlled chemical short-range order (CSRO) via a low-temperature aging treatment will enhance the dynamic mechanical performance (strength and ductility balance) of Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy under high strain rates and elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy (e.g., Fe25Ni27Cr18Mn28 at.%) in a single-phase FCC polycrystalline state with large grain size (hundreds of micrometers) and minimal porosity, as prepared by arc-melting and homogenization.
generation.intervention: Low-temperature aging treatment (e.g., 500-700°C for 10-50 hours) to induce chemical short-range order (CSRO) without forming long-range ordered precipitates or secondary phases.
generation.conditions: Dynamic loading conditions: strain rates ranging from 10^3 to 10^4 s^-1 (split-Hopkinson pressure bar regime) and temperatures from 300 K to 800 K.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemical short-range order (CSRO) clusters that act as obstacles to dislocation motion, increasing resistance to plastic deformation while maintaining sufficient ductility through localized strain hardening mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: CSRO introduces local chemical fluctuations that increase the local stacking fault energy (SFE) and create short-range barriers to dislocation glide, thereby enhancing yield strength and strain hardening capacity under dynamic loading. The ordered clusters impede dislocation motion more effectively than random solid solution, leading to improved strength-ductility synergy at high strain rates where thermal activation is limited.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aged FeNiCrMn alloy will exhibit a 15-25% increase in dynamic yield strength and a 10-20% improvement in energy absorption capacity compared to the unaged alloy at strain rates >10^3 s^-1 and temperatures up to 800 K, while maintaining or slightly improving ductility (elongation to fracture) due to enhanced strain hardening.
generation.baseline: Unaged Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy with random atomic distribution, showing moderate strength but limited strain hardening under dynamic loading, particularly at elevated temperatures where thermal activation reduces flow stress.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only within the aging temperature range of 500-700°C and time range of 10-50 hours; excessive aging leading to long-range ordering or precipitate formation will degrade ductility. The benefit is most pronounced at strain rates >10^3 s^-1 and temperatures <800 K; at very high temperatures (>800 K), thermal activation may dominate and reduce the CSRO effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of CSRO-induced strengthening is uncertain due to limited direct experimental data on FeNiCrMn under dynamic loading. The optimal aging parameters may vary based on initial microstructure and trace impurities. The interaction between CSRO and deformation twinning or martensitic transformation under dynamic conditions is not fully characterized.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform split-Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) tests on aged (500-700°C, 10-50h) and unaged FeNiCrMn samples at strain rates of 10^3, 10^4 s^-1 and temperatures of 300, 500, 700, 800 K. Measure dynamic yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to fracture. Use atom probe tomography (APT) to quantify CSRO in aged samples. If the aged samples show no significant improvement (>5%) in strength-ductility balance compared to unaged samples, or if APT reveals no CSRO formation, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. The response of atoms to cluster or order in alloys offers deep insights to the microstructural behavior. This trend is particularly important for multi-component alloys, because the ordering can drive the system to various microstructural states, such as crystalline or intermetallic solids, from the disordered FCC ( A1 ), BCC ( A2 ), or HCP ( A3 ) conditions. In Al x CrCoFeNi, the Al content can influence the final structural configuration [6] [23] [24] [25] [26] [27] due to the larger atom size, compared to other constituents, which considerably changes the lattice ordering. When the mole fraction of Al <0.3, a single-phase A1 is observed, and a single-phase A2 is found for Al >1.17, while a two-phase ( A1 + A2 ) for 0.3 ≤ Al ≤1.17 is reported [24] [26] . Using the methods and approximations for accurate estimates of the formation enthalpy and relative energy of A1 and A2 phases [28] , the first-principles KKR-CPA results in Fig. 2 for Al of 0 < x < 2 mole fractions predict a similar global stability found in the experiment, i.e., A1 for x < 0.5, A1 + A2 for 0.5 ≤ Al ≤1.25, and A2 for Al > 1.25. Nanomaterials are new age materials exhibiting exceptional mechanical, electronic, and optical properties due to their unique structure and high surface-area to volume ratio [ [1] ]. Among nanomaterials, one dimensional (1D) metallic nanowires (NWs) are widely used for different applications including nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, energy harvesting and storage, ultrasensitive sensing, and nanoelectromechanical devices [ [2] , [3] , [4] ]. At the nanoscale, 1D NWs usually exhibit ultra high strength, differently from bulk materials, which makes them ideal candidates for studying their fundamental deformation mechanisms. Dislocation nucleation from free surfaces and its subsequent propagation through NWs has been found to be a dominant deformation mechanism in metallic NWs such as Au, Ag, Cu, and Ni [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. This enables reorientation to a more preferred phase, resulting in exceptional mechanical properties such as superplasticity, high yielding strength, pseudoelasticity, and shape memory effects [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ].
